# Welcome {-}

```{r include = FALSE}
# Bibliography of R packages used to build the book
knitr::write_bib(c("bookdown", "knitr", "rmarkdown", "ggplot2", "DiagrammeR",
                   "kableExtra", "visNetwork", "DT"), "packages.bib")
```

::: {.cover-hero}
```{r cover, echo = FALSE, out.width = "100%"}
knitr::include_graphics("images/cover.png")
```
:::

**Social Science Theory** is an open-access field guide to the ideas that social
scientists and evidence-minded managers use to explain behaviour: of people,
teams, firms, markets, and societies. It covers more than one hundred theories,
effects, and frameworks drawn from management, marketing, economics, psychology,
sociology, communication, and information systems.

Every chapter is written to be useful twice: once for **research** (what the
theory claims, why, under which conditions, how it has been tested, and how to
derive hypotheses from it) and once for **practice** (where the theory shows up in
real business decisions, and what it implies for strategy, marketing, finance,
operations, and people management).

```{r tab-preface-contents}
atlas <- readr::read_csv("data/theory-atlas.csv", show_col_types = FALSE)
atlas |>
  dplyr::count(part, name = "Entries") |>
  dplyr::mutate(part = factor(part, levels = c("Foundations", "Organizations & Strategy",
                                               "Individuals & Groups",
                                               "Effects, Phenomena & Frameworks"))) |>
  dplyr::arrange(part) |>
  dplyr::mutate(Chapters = c("1-3", "4-10", "11-17", "18-20"),
                `What you will find` = c(
                  "What theory is, how to evaluate it, and how to turn it into hypotheses",
                  "Resources, capabilities, governance, institutions, information, networks, diffusion",
                  "Culture, motivation, self-regulation, social influence, decisions, emotion, persuasion",
                  "Named effects, social phenomena, classic models, and a cross-theory mechanism toolkit")) |>
  dplyr::select(Part = part, Chapters, Entries, `What you will find`) |>
  book_table(caption = "What is inside the book.")
```

## Who this book is for {-}

- **Doctoral students and early-career researchers** who need a systematic map of
  the theories their field "just knows", and a fast way to find the right lens for
  a research question.
- **Faculty** looking for a free, citable companion text for seminars in
  management, marketing, organizational behaviour, and consumer behaviour.
- **Practitioners**, strategists, marketers, product managers, analysts, HR
  leaders, and consultants, who want to understand *why* interventions work,
  not just *that* they work.

## How each chapter is built {-}

Theories are presented in a consistent format so they can be compared at a
glance:

::: {.theory-card}
**Core claim**: the theory in one or two sentences. **Origins**, who proposed
it, when, and in which discipline. **Level of analysis**: individual, dyad,
group, firm, market, or institution. **Key constructs** and **boundary
conditions**. **Related theories**: links to neighbouring entries.
:::

Each card is followed by the theory's **core logic and propositions**, a
**mechanism diagram**, a review of **evidence and extensions**, a balanced
discussion of **critiques** (including replication status where relevant),
one or more **business cases**, and a **research toolkit** with sample hypotheses,
measures, designs, and data sources. Chapters close with key takeaways, a
comparison table, discussion questions, and annotated further reading.

Look for these boxes throughout:

::: {.business-case}
Applications drawn from strategy, marketing, finance, operations, HR, and policy.
:::

::: {.research-toolkit}
Sample hypotheses, operationalizations, research designs, and data sources.
:::

::: {.debate}
Critiques, contested findings, and replication evidence.
:::

::: {.pitfall}
The most common ways a theory is misunderstood or misapplied.
:::

## How to read this book {-}

You do not need to read it in order. If you have a specific theory in mind, use
the search bar or jump straight to the [Theory Atlas](#theory-atlas), a
searchable table of every entry with its level of analysis, mechanism, key
source, and business use. If you want the big picture, start with the
[Introduction](#intro) and the interactive [theory map](#theory-map). If you are
writing a paper, Chapters \@ref(what-is-theory) and \@ref(using-theory) show how
to move from a theory to testable hypotheses.

If this book is useful in your work, please cite it:

> Nguyen, M. (`r format(Sys.Date(), "%Y")`). *Social Science Theory: A Field Guide to the
> Theories, Effects, and Frameworks Behind Research and Business*.
> https://mikenguyen13.github.io/social-theory/

```
@book{nguyen_social_theory,
  author = {Nguyen, Mike},

            and Frameworks Behind Research and Business},
  year   = {`r format(Sys.Date(), "%Y")`},

```

## Contributing {-}

This is a living book. Corrections, new theories, better examples, and
translations are welcome. Every page has an **Edit this page** link that opens
the source on GitHub. You can also open an
[issue](https://github.com/mikenguyen13/social-theory/issues) to suggest a theory.
Contributors should follow the
[style guide](https://github.com/mikenguyen13/social-theory/blob/master/STYLE_GUIDE.md).
If the book helps you, starring the
[GitHub repository](https://github.com/mikenguyen13/social-theory) helps others
find it.

## About the author {-}

Mike Nguyen is the author of the open-source *A Guide on Data Analysis*, a
companion text on statistical methods and causal inference for social science
research. This book began as his own systematic notes on the theories that
researchers in business and the social sciences are expected to know, and has
grown into a reference for students, scholars, and practitioners.

The book is written in [R Markdown](https://rmarkdown.rstudio.com) and built with
